lines: A dashboard's daily number comes from averaging a day's worth of hourly averages together.
One of those hours happened right after a restart and only had a tiny handful of readings in it.
That thin hour still counted exactly as much in the average as every single full, ordinary hour did.
Some summaries can be combined cleanly: take two of them and produce the exact summary of everything they covered together.
A minimum, a maximum, a running total, and a plain count all behave this way.
A percentile doesn't. There's no rule anywhere for combining two separate percentiles into the percentile of everything combined.
Worth reasoning through before the next reveal answers it.
Two of these hourly summaries, each storing a running total and a count instead of a plain average, get combined into one.
Does that combined result match exactly what computing straight from every individual reading would give?
answer: A running total and a count already hold everything there is to know about their own hour, so combining them throws nothing away that an average would have already lost.

lines: Put it to the test directly.
The combined running total and the combined count land exactly on the true total and the true count from every reading.
Averaging the hourly averages together, by contrast, lands nowhere close.
A reading that shows up only after its hour has already been summarized still has to change something.
It changes that one hour's maximum, its count, and its average, all at once.
Every other hour that already had its summary computed stays completely untouched by it.
Keep the full-detail readings for a matter of days, a coarser one-minute summary for months, and an even coarser one-hour summary stretching back years.
A question about the last few hours reads straight from the full-detail data. A question spanning years reads from the coarsest summary available.
A question that spans both ranges at once has to read from two different summaries and stitch the two together into one answer.
A single genuine spike buried inside one hour's worth of readings barely nudges that hour's average at all.
The exact same hour's maximum shows that same spike in full, completely unchanged.
Only a summary that can be combined from two partial pieces survives being rolled up at all; an average gets derived from a total and a count, never stored on its own.
A reading arriving late still has to reopen the one summary it belongs to.
A spanning question has no choice but to stitch summaries together, and an average and a maximum simply keep two different truths.
One more case worth reasoning through before moving on.
A dashboard reports a single daily average with no record anywhere of how many readings went into each hour behind that number.
Is that daily average trustworthy all on its own, with nothing else to check it against?
answer: Without each hour's own count sitting next to it, a thin, barely-sampled hour and a completely full, ordinary hour look exactly identical inside that one daily figure.
